title: Cookie
summary:
A cookie is **one `name=value` string** that the server asks the browser to keep (via `Set-Cookie`) and that the browser then attaches **automatically** to every matching request: `Cookie: session_id=abc123; theme=dark`. A request can carry several cookies, each its own pair. It is the one browser storage the **server sees on every request**, which is why it carries session IDs and why it is a poor place for bulk data.

**Identity** is the triple (name, Domain, Path). Two cookies coexist if they differ in name or path:

```http
Set-Cookie: session=abc; Domain=example.com; Path=/
Set-Cookie: session=xyz; Domain=example.com; Path=/admin
```

A request to `/admin/users` sends both; one to `/home` sends only the first.

Attributes that matter:
- `Domain` and `Path`: scope. With no `Domain` the cookie is host-only; with `Domain=example.com` it is also sent to subdomains.
- `Expires` or `Max-Age`: a persistent cookie. Without them it is a **session cookie**, dropped when the browser session ends.
- `Secure`: HTTPS only. `HttpOnly`: invisible to JavaScript, blunting XSS theft. `SameSite=Lax|Strict|None`: limits cross-site sending, the main CSRF defence.

Limits: about 4 KB per cookie, and every byte rides on every request in scope, including images. Use cookies for small identifiers (an opaque session ID or a signed token); keep everything else on the server or in [localStorage](#/sd/f/local-storage).

drills.q: The browser holds `session=abc; Domain=example.com; Path=/` and `session=xyz; Domain=example.com; Path=/admin`. It requests `https://example.com/admin/users`. What does the `Cookie` header contain?
options: Both `session=xyz` and `session=abc`, since both scopes match (the server should not rely on their order)
drills.explain: Name, domain and path make two distinct cookies. Both path scopes match `/admin/users`, so both are sent (more specific path first by convention). Request `/home` and only `session=abc` goes along.

drills.q: Select all measures that are appropriate for the session cookie of a banking site.
options: `Secure`, so it is never sent over plain HTTP
`HttpOnly`, so injected scripts cannot read it
`SameSite=Lax` (or Strict), to limit cross-site requests carrying it
drills.explain: Setting `Domain` widens exposure to every subdomain (including a neglected one); leave the cookie host-only unless you need sharing.

drills.q: A page makes 60 requests to the same domain, including images and scripts. The browser attaches 8 cookies totalling 3 KB to each of them. How many KB of cookie data are uploaded for that page load?
drills.explain: 3 KB x 60 = 180 KB upload, none of it useful for static assets. Serve static files from a cookieless domain, or keep cookie payloads tiny.

drills.q: A server-rendered app needs to know who the user is on the very first request of every page. Where should the session identifier live?
options: A cookie, because the browser sends it automatically even on the first navigation request, before any script has run
localStorage, read by script and added as a header
drills.explain: Only cookies travel with navigations by themselves. localStorage is invisible to the server until JavaScript copies it. Query parameters leak into logs and referrers.

drills.q: Compare cookies with localStorage on three axes: who can see them, when they are sent, and how much they hold.
drills.answer: **Cookies** are sent by the browser to the server on every matching request, are readable by the server (and by scripts unless `HttpOnly`), and hold about 4 KB each. **localStorage** is never sent anywhere, is readable by scripts on the same origin only, and holds roughly 5 MB. Use cookies for small server-visible identifiers such as a session ID, and localStorage for client-only preferences or caches.
